[![Node CI](https://github.com/nodejs/undici/actions/workflows/nodejs.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/nodejs/undici/actions/workflows/nodejs.yml) [![js-standard-style](https://img.shields.io/badge/code%20style-standard-brightgreen.svg?style=flat)](http://standardjs.com/) [![npm version](https://badge.fury.io/js/undici.svg)](https://badge.fury.io/js/undici) [![codecov](https://codecov.io/gh/nodejs/undici/branch/main/graph/badge.svg?token=yZL6LtXkOA)](https://codecov.io/gh/nodejs/undici)

An HTTP/1.1 client, written from scratch for Node.js.

> Undici means eleven in Italian. 1.1 -> 11 -> Eleven -> Undici.
It is also a Stranger Things reference.

## How to get involved

Have a question about using Undici? Open a [Q&A Discussion](https://github.com/nodejs/undici/discussions/new) or join our official OpenJS [Slack](https://openjs-foundation.slack.com/archives/C01QF9Q31QD) channel.

Looking to contribute? Start by reading the [contributing guide](./CONTRIBUTING.md)

## Install

```
npm i undici
```

## Benchmarks

The benchmark is a simple getting data [example](https://github.com/nodejs/undici/blob/main/benchmarks/benchmark.js) using a
50 TCP connections with a pipelining depth of 10 running on Node 20.10.0.

|  undici - request   |    10     | 19264.24 req/sec |  ± 1.74 %   |        + 420.03 %         |

Audit complete. `findings.json` is written at the repo root (the only file I created; all PoC scripts went to `$TMPDIR`).

## What I reviewed
This is **undici** (Node.js HTTP/1.1+fetch client, `package.json` says 6.11.0). First-party code = `lib/`, `index.js`, `index-fetch.js`, `scripts/`, `build/`; I skipped `deps/llhttp`, the wasm blobs, and `test/wpt`. No network access, so I couldn't diff against the published tarball — instead I read the security-critical paths, and additionally ran the repo's own test suite (121+ files passed) against a local shim for the missing `@matteo.collina/tspl` dep to rule out regressions in covered behaviour, then probed the library with raw-TCP servers to confirm each finding on the wire.

Several classes in your list have no attack surface here: no SQL, no `eval`/template engines, no XML parsing (no XXE), no filesystem access from `lib/` (no path traversal), and no HTML rendering (no XSS). Header-name, header-value, `path`, `method` and `host` validation all held up under fuzzing, as did multipart escaping of field names/filenames.

## Findings (4)

1. **CRLF injection / request splitting via the `upgrade` option** — `lib/dispatcher/client-h1.js:972-974` (CWE-93). Every other value interpolated into the raw request is validated; `upgrade` is only type-checked (`lib/core/request.js:64`). PoC via `client.upgrade({ protocol: ... })` put **two complete requests** on the socket.

2. **`proxy-authorization` leaked across origins on redirect** — `lib/handler/redirect-handler.js:197-209` (CWE-200). `shouldRemoveHeader` strips only `host`/`authorization`/`cookie`. PoC: after a 302 to a second origin, `authorization` and `cookie` were gone but `proxy-authorization: Basic …` arrived at the attacker origin. The equivalent `fetch` path *does* delete it, so this is an inconsistency, not a design choice.

3. **Unvalidated blob `type` injected into multipart bodies** — `lib/web/fetch/body.js:130-134` (CWE-93). `FileLike` copies `options.type` with the spec's sanitisation left as a `TODO` (`lib/web/fetch/file.js:119-120`), so a duck-typed blob-like with a CRLF-bearing `type` injects extra form parts. PoC produced an attacker-controlled `admin=true` field. Precondition: the app passes a blob-like whose `type` came from untrusted data — plausible in forwarding/proxy code, which is why I included it, but it's the weakest of the four.

4. **Trustworthy-origin check uses a substring match** — `lib/web/fetch/util.js:534-538` (CWE-346). `hostname.includes('localhost.')` makes `http://localhost.attacker.com` and `http://my-localhost.evil.net` "potentially trustworthy", defeating the referrer-downgrade suppression in `determineRequestsReferrer` under the default `strict-origin-when-cross-origin` policy.

One thing I looked at and deliberately left out: two response headers named `__proto__` make `parseHeaders` throw `val.push is not a function`, but it's caught and only fails that one request, so it isn't a usable DoS.
